messages.author: e1c430550f86b1f6
messages.subject: multivariate regression help
parts:
Hi all,

I am trying to play with fitting a linear model with M-coefficients being drawn from a multi-normal prior (a dump version of the sample from manual) and N sets of observations

STAN code, R data and results are attached.

Four Questions:

Q1. During the fitting process, I noticed the engine through out a lot of rejection messages (mostly during warmup, but also occasionally during sampling)

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
stan::prob::lkj_corr_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): y is not positive definite. y(0,0) is 1:0
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

However:

a. Rhat seems ok, except one of the omega has NaN
b. the coefficient posterior seems reasonable resemble that from a simple multiple regression (the 2 coefficients are quite independent).

So, going back to the error messages:  Is that due to my model specification or lack of data or nothing to worry about?

Q2. This is a bit of generalization question: For a model with M-coefficients, what's the typical size needed for N (observation sizes)? In my problem domain, N is not large - in the order of 10s. I'm trying to get a sense of realistically, how many predictors I can use.

Q3. I tried to do the cholesky factorization (code attached: multi_norm_ch.stan) and the engine now spills out *a lot* of messages complaining beta being negative:

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
Invalid value of beta: validate transformed params(N4stan5agrad3varE): beta[2] is -3.27553:0, but must be greater than or equal to 0
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

I would guess the issue is that I have beta lower bounded at 0 and the computation in the transformed parameters can volatile that.

Question is: what should i do in the transformed parameter block to ensure lower bound is not violated?


Q4: I would like to use the model to do posterior prediction. In the generated quantities block, is following sufficient if I want to take in consideration of the covariance.

eal y_tilde;
y_tilde <- normal_rng (X_tilde * beta, sigma);
(assuming X_tilde is now supplied)


Many thanks,

Andy

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: some general Stan advice
parts: Hi, see responses below.

> On Apr 21, 2015, at 3:56 AM, andy...@cubist-asia.com wrote:
>
> Hi all,
>
> I am trying to play with fitting a linear model with M-coefficients being drawn from a multi-normal prior (a dump version of the sample from manual) and N sets of observations
>
> STAN code, R data and results are attached.
>
> Four Questions:
>
> Q1. During the fitting process, I noticed the engine through out a lot of rejection messages (mostly during warmup, but also occasionally during sampling)
>
> Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
> stan::prob::lkj_corr_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): y is not positive definite. y(0,0) is 1:0
> If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
> but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

This is ok but it is worth looking back at the model to make sure it makes sense. We recommend the usual steps:

- Build up your final model, starting with something smaller that you understand well, then adding features one by one and digesting each step. We call this the network of models.

- Fake-data checking, where you simulate data from the model and then fit the model to the data and check that you can (approximately) recover the original parameters. We have a vision of implementing this semi-automatically using a graphical model wrapper in R/Python/Julia/etc but we’re not there yet.

>
> However:
>
> a. Rhat seems ok, except one of the omega has NaN
Nan isn’t good; you should check that!

> b. the coefficient posterior seems reasonable resemble that from a simple multiple regression (the 2 coefficients are quite independent).
>
> So, going back to the error messages: Is that due to my model specification or lack of data or nothing to worry about?
>
> Q2. This is a bit of generalization question: For a model with M-coefficients, what's the typical size needed for N (observation sizes)? In my problem domain, N is not large - in the order of 10s. I’m trying to get a sense of realistically, how many predictors I can use.

The larger M, the stronger a prior you’ll need. We’ve been moving toward routinely using informative priors (my current favorite is to give everything N(0,1) on the unconstrained scale by default, assuming that the model has been scaled so that parameters are roughly of order 1 (so, for example, in a regression, you want your predictors to be of order 1, nothing like .000324 or 7383249).

> Q3. I tried to do the cholesky factorization (code attached: multi_norm_ch.stan) and the engine now spills out *a lot* of messages complaining beta being negative:
>
> Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
> Invalid value of beta: validate transformed params(N4stan5agrad3varE): beta[2] is -3.27553:0, but must be greater than or equal to 0
> If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
> but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
>
> I would guess the issue is that I have beta lower bounded at 0 and the computation in the transformed parameters can volatile that.
>
> Question is: what should i do in the transformed parameter block to ensure lower bound is not violated?

In general I think it’s a bad idea to bound parameters like this. If a parameter has a natural bound, sure (for example, scale parameters must be positive, probabilities must be between 0 and 1, correlations must be between -1 and 1, etc). But if you just want a coefficient to be positive, don’t use a hard bound; instead use a soft constraint, e.g. a N(1,1) prior.

> Q4: I would like to use the model to do posterior prediction. In the generated quantities block, is following sufficient if I want to take in consideration of the covariance.
>
> real y_tilde;

> y_tilde <- normal_rng (X_tilde * beta, sigma);
> (assuming X_tilde is now supplied)
Yes, it’s that simple!

If it's a correlation matrix, that's by design. The 1 values
on the diagonals don't move, so you get a 0/0 in the formula.
It's been confusing users, though --- what should we do here?
The problem is that we don't know if it's because a parameter is
stuck because it's not sampling or stuck by design, so I'd be
reluctant to just put it to the max value by default.

>>
>> real y_tilde;

>
> Yes, it’s that simple!

That'll take into account the covariance for beta and sigma.

- bob

messages.subject: Re: some general Stan advice
parts:
Hi, I don’t know enough about your model to say, but there are different sorts of theoretical constraints.  Sometimes you have a true constraint, for example you have a model E(y) = exp(-a*x), and x can be arbitrarily large, so “a” must be positive.  Other times it’s not a true constraint, for example you have an econ model with an elatisticity parameter and for theroetical reasons you think it must be postive.  Here I think it’s better not to put in a hard constraint but instead to let the data speak.
A

messages.subject: Re: some general Stan advice
parts:
Hi - it's indeed an elasticity parameter of an econ model, such that I would have expected either:

a) the dependent variable to co-move with the predictors (i.e. +ve value)
b) the dependent variable cannot explain by the predictors (i.e. 0)

Furthermore, the size of our data set is rather constrained - teens at best, quite often, upper single digit and can contain outliers, either due to typo in data collection (i.e. the outlier shouldn't be there) or other situational idiosyncratic issues (i.e. the outlier should be there).

We are quite new to STAN and Bayesian. In the past, I have used simple OLS tools and found that these issues could  cause the engine to come up with -ve elasticity parameters. Hence, I have adopted the lower bound at 0. What would have been a more "native" Bayesian to handle this (or, it wouldn't really be an issue with Bayesian/STAN since the posterior would have captured this)?

Andy

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: some general Stan advice
parts:
Hi, I’d suggest an informative prior, for example if you think the elasticity should be between 0 and 1, you could use a normal prior with mean 0.5 and sd 0.5.  The point is that you’d like to let the data speak but at the same time you want to control your estimate.  If you do get a negative elasticity estimate, so be it (sometimes such things can happen due to unforeseen interactions in the data) but then you’ll probably also have a big standard error.  And if the data really “want” to find a negative elasticity with a small s.e., you’d like to know this—as, at the very least, this will tell you that there’s something weird about the data.  Better to let the data speak than to get an estimate right on the boundary which still doesn’t fit the data.

A

Note to Bob:  We should throw this advice into whatever file we’re keeping with general advice, so we can throw it into the forthcoming book!

In general I think it’s a bad idea to bound parameters like this.  If a parameter has a natural bound, sure (for example, scale parameters must be positive, probabilities must be between 0 and 1, correlations must be between -1 and 1, etc).  But if you just want a coefficient to be positive, don’t use a hard bound; instead use a soft constraint, e.g. a N(1,1) prior.

> Q4: I would like to use the model to do posterior prediction. In the generated quantities block, is following sufficient if I want to take in consideration of the covariance.
>
> real y_tilde;
> y_tilde <- normal_rng (X_tilde * beta, sigma);
> (assuming X_tilde is now supplied)

Yes, it’s that simple!

parts:
> On Apr 24, 2015, at 2:05 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> Hi, I’d suggest an informative prior, for example if you think the elasticity should be between 0 and 1, you could use a normal prior with mean 0.5 and sd 0.5. The point is that you’d like to let the data speak but at the same time you want to control your estimate. If you do get a negative elasticity estimate, so be it (sometimes such things can happen due to unforeseen interactions in the data) but then you’ll probably also have a big standard error. And if the data really “want” to find a negative elasticity with a small s.e., you’d like to know this—as, at the very least, this will tell you that there’s something weird about the data. Better to let the data speak than to get an estimate right on the boundary which still doesn’t fit the data.

parts:
> On Apr 24, 2015, at 1:42 PM, andy...@cubist-asia.com wrote:
>
> Hi - it's indeed an elasticity parameter of an econ model, such that I would have expected either:
>
> a) the dependent variable to co-move with the predictors (i.e. +ve value)
> b) the dependent variable cannot explain by the predictors (i.e. 0)
>
> Furthermore, the size of our data set is rather constrained - teens at best, quite often, upper single digit and can contain outliers, either due to typo in data collection (i.e. the outlier shouldn't be there) or other situational idiosyncratic issues (i.e. the outlier should be there).
>
> We are quite new to STAN and Bayesian. In the past, I have used simple OLS tools and found that these issues could cause the engine to come up with -ve elasticity parameters. Hence, I have adopted the lower bound at 0. What would have been a more "native" Bayesian to handle this (or, it wouldn't really be an issue with Bayesian/STAN since the posterior would have captured this)?

If you have outliers in the data due to data collection, then
you either want to move to a full measurement-error model where
you model the errors, or you can hack it in the existing model
by making a more robust noise model (such as a Student-t of low
degrees of freedom).

You can also add penalties for OLS --- Stan also has a penalized maximum
likelihood estimator.

- Bob
